title: Income variability and price pressure convert household room into overlapping substitutions, delay, debt, and extra work
source_unit: Federal Reserve 2025 Survey of Household Economics and Decisionmaking income, help, and price-adaptation module

observations.period: 2025 SHED survey and reference year; published 2026

denominator.unit: U.S. adult respondents; denominators vary across income variability, outside help, budget margin, and price-response questions

income_variability.unit: percent reporting income varying at least occasionally

variability_bill_difficulty.unit: percent reporting income variability made it difficult to pay bills

outside_help.unit: percent reporting outside help with a listed expense

money_left_over.value: 19% below $25,000 family income versus 59% at $100,000 or more reporting money left over always or often

price_adaptations.value: 62% switched to cheaper products; 60% used less or stopped use; 46% delayed a major purchase; 41% reduced saving; 16% borrowed more; 17% worked more or got another job

protected_or_sacrificed_outcome.unit: missing named bill, purchase, quality, care, health, time, debt-repayment, provider, remedy, trust, and exit outcome for the same respondent episode

mechanism.value: Households can preserve current consumption by transferring pressure into lower-quality purchases, reduced use, delay, lower saving, debt, additional work, or outside help; the cross-sectional survey cannot identify the sequence or durability

observations.method: Structured extraction from the Federal Reserve's official 2025 SHED income-and-expenses report; question-specific universes and overlapping adaptation categories are retained separately rather than treated as a causal pathway.
observations.uncertainty: The survey does not link a respondent across a dated bill or price episode to payment completion, amount, liquid buffer, debt terms, care obligations, schedule control, provider response, remedy, trust, switching, or exit. Price-response categories overlap and may reflect smoothing, deprivation, preference, or mixed motives.
observations.subgroup: U.S. adults, with published income-patterned budget-margin estimates; no linked household episode, geography, race, care, health, or work subgroup is retained here.
observations.counterinterpretation: Working more can protect current spending while reducing care or rest; outside help can buffer a bill without creating durable room; switching to cheaper goods can reflect agency, constraint, or both.

boundary: This record establishes descriptive household income variability, outside help, budget margin, and price adaptations. It does not establish a dated causal shock, protected payment, durable security, or household recovery.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The hash covers the compact project event ledger derived from official Federal Reserve SHED tables and report; SHED microdata and respondent identifiers are not retained.
